title: The knee joint
summary: Two condyles on a flat plateau, held together by ligaments and menisci.

steps.title: A hinge that is not a hinge
steps.text: Two convex femoral condyles roll and glide on an almost flat tibial plateau, with the patella as a sesamoid in the quadriceps tendon increasing its lever arm. Almost all the stability is ligamentous, which is why the knee is the most commonly injured large joint.

check.q: What makes the knee stable despite having two round condyles on a flat plateau?
check.a: The ligaments, the menisci and the muscles — very little bony congruence.

steps.title: The cruciates
steps.text:
Named for their tibial attachments.
Anterior cruciate runs up, back and laterally; it stops the tibia sliding forwards – tested by the anterior drawer and Lachman tests. It tears with a twisting, decelerating injury, often with an audible pop and a rapid haemarthrosis.
Posterior cruciate runs up, forwards and medially; it stops the tibia sliding backwards – the dashboard injury.

check.q: Which cruciate stops the tibia sliding forwards, and which test detects its rupture?
check.a: The anterior cruciate ligament; the anterior drawer and Lachman tests.

steps.title: The menisci
steps.text:
Two C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges deepening the plateau and spreading load. The medial meniscus is less mobile because it is attached to the tibial collateral ligament – hence the classic 'unhappy triad' of medial meniscus, tibial collateral ligament and anterior cruciate.

Only the outer third has a blood supply, so peripheral tears can be repaired and central ones cannot.

check.q: Why does the medial meniscus tear more often than the lateral?
check.a: It is attached to the medial collateral ligament and so is less mobile.

steps.title: The collaterals and locking
steps.text:
The tibial (medial) collateral is a flat band blended with the capsule and meniscus; the fibular (lateral) collateral is a cord standing free of the capsule.

In full extension the femur medially rotates on the tibia and the ligaments tighten – the knee locks. Popliteus unlocks it by laterally rotating the femur before flexion can begin.
focus: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

check.q: Which muscle unlocks the extended knee?
check.a: Popliteus, by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia.

focus: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
steps.title: Locking depends on which bone is fixed
steps.text:
The rotation described earlier assumed a foot planted on the ground. As that knee reaches full extension, the femur rotates medially on the fixed tibia. Sit with the foot free instead, and the same relative movement is described as the tibia rotating laterally on the femur.

Popliteus reverses this screw-home movement to begin flexion: it laterally rotates the femur in standing, or medially rotates the tibia when the leg is free. Before naming a rotation, identify the bone that is moving. Otherwise two correct descriptions of one mechanism can sound like a contradiction.

check.q: With the foot off the ground, how does popliteus begin to unlock the knee?
check.a: It medially rotates the tibia relative to the femur.

steps.title: Why the patella improves the pull
steps.text:
The patella is embedded in the quadriceps tendon, with the patellar ligament continuing below it to the tibial tuberosity. By holding the tendon away from the knee's axis, it increases the extensor mechanism's moment arm. The same muscle force can therefore generate more extension torque.

As the knee bends, the patella tracks in the femoral trochlear groove and its contact region changes. The quadriceps tendon, patella, patellar ligament and tibial tuberosity make one continuous force pathway. Interrupt that pathway at any point and active knee extension can fail, even if the femoral and tibial articular surfaces remain aligned.

check.q: What mechanical advantage does the patella give quadriceps?
check.a: It increases the distance between the tendon and the joint axis, increasing the moment arm for knee extension.

objectives: Name the ligaments of the knee and the movement each resists
Explain the role of the menisci and why the medial one tears more often
Describe the screw-home mechanism
Explain knee locking with either the foot fixed or the tibia free to move
takeaways: ACL resists anterior translation of the tibia; PCL resists posterior.
The medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament, so they tear together.
The knee locks in extension by lateral rotation of the tibia and is unlocked by popliteus.
Terminal extension externally rotates a free tibia; with the foot planted the femur internally rotates instead. Popliteus reverses the relative rotation.

title: The shoulder joint
summary: Maximum range, minimum stability – and what that costs.

steps.title: A golf ball on a tee
steps.text: The humeral head is three or four times the area of the glenoid, which is deepened only a little by the fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum. Stability comes from the rotator cuff and the capsule rather than from bone.

check.q: How much of the humeral head is in contact with the glenoid at any time?
check.a: About a third.

steps.title: Why it dislocates forwards and down
steps.text:
The capsule is reinforced in front by the glenohumeral ligaments and above by coracohumeral fibres, but its inferior part is lax and unsupported – the weak point.

Over 95% of dislocations are anteroinferior. A Bankart lesion tears the anterior labrum; a Hill–Sachs lesion dents the posterolateral humeral head. Look for axillary nerve injury: weak abduction and a numb regimental badge patch.

check.q: In which direction does the shoulder usually dislocate, and which nerve must you test?
check.a: Anteroinferiorly; test the axillary nerve.

steps.title: Scapulohumeral rhythm
steps.text:
Of 180° of abduction, only about 120° happens at the glenohumeral joint; the rest is scapular rotation on the chest wall, driven by trapezius and serratus anterior, in roughly a 2:1 ratio.

Long thoracic nerve injury paralyses serratus anterior and gives a winged scapula with loss of abduction above the horizontal.

check.q: What is the scapulohumeral rhythm?
check.a: About 2° of glenohumeral movement for every 1° of scapular rotation.

steps.title: The capsule needs a spare fold
steps.text:
With the arm at the side, the inferior shoulder capsule forms a loose axillary recess. As the arm abducts this fold opens out, allowing the humeral head to move without immediately pulling the capsule tight. Laxity here is part of normal mobility.

A thickened, contracted capsule loses that reserve. The result can be restriction of both active movement and passive movement, with external rotation particularly limited in adhesive capsulitis. Compare this with weakness alone: a weak muscle may fail to raise the arm even when an examiner can still move the joint through a larger range.

check.q: Why does capsular shortening restrict passive as well as active shoulder movement?
check.a: The shortened capsule physically limits the joint excursion regardless of who supplies the force.

steps.title: Which part of the shoulder is moving?
steps.text:
Watch the scapula while imagining an arm being raised. Early and late portions of elevation do not maintain a perfectly fixed ratio; the familiar 2:1 rhythm is a useful overall approximation. The scapula rotates upwards while the humerus moves relative to the glenoid.

If the glenohumeral joint is stiff, a person may compensate by lifting and rotating the whole shoulder girdle. The hand still rises, but that does not prove that the ball-and-socket joint has moved normally. Follow the scapular border as well as the humerus when explaining the motion.

check.q: Why can lifting the hand high conceal a stiff glenohumeral joint?
check.a: Extra scapular and shoulder-girdle movement can compensate for reduced movement between the humerus and glenoid.

objectives: Describe the bony and soft tissue stabilisers of the shoulder
Explain why anterior dislocation is so common
Name the structures at risk in a dislocation
Distinguish movement at the glenohumeral joint from movement of the scapula and explain the capsule's inferior fold
takeaways: A shallow glenoid buys range at the cost of stability.
The capsule is weakest inferiorly, so the head dislocates anteroinferiorly.
Check the axillary nerve before and after reduction.
Arm elevation uses both scapular and glenohumeral movement; the inferior capsular recess unfolds as the arm rises.

title: The hip joint
summary: Built for stability, and a blood supply that punishes a fracture.

steps.title: A deep socket
steps.text: The acetabulum takes nearly half the femoral head and is deepened further by the acetabular labrum. The capsule runs from the acetabular rim to the intertrochanteric line in front, but only to the middle of the femoral neck behind – so the posterior neck is partly extracapsular.

check.q: Which is the strongest ligament in the body, and what does it prevent?
check.a: The iliofemoral ligament — it prevents hyperextension and lets you stand without muscular effort.

steps.title: Blood supply and the fractured neck
steps.text:
The head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck under the capsule, plus a small and usually inadequate artery in the ligament of the head.

An intracapsular fracture tears those retinacular vessels, so the head dies: avascular necrosis. That is why an intracapsular fracture in an older patient is usually replaced rather than fixed, while an extracapsular one is fixed.

check.q: Why does an intracapsular femoral neck fracture threaten the head?
check.a: It tears the retinacular vessels that run up the neck from the medial circumflex femoral artery.

steps.title: The abductors and the Trendelenburg sign
steps.text: Gluteus medius and minimus hold the pelvis level when you stand on one leg. If they fail – superior gluteal nerve palsy, a painful hip, a dislocated hip or a fracture – the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side, and the patient lurches over the affected hip to compensate.

check.q: A patient stands on the left leg and the right hip drops. Which muscles are weak and on which side?
check.a: The left gluteus medius and minimus — the standing side.

steps.title: Why standing uses so little effort
steps.text:
The capsule is reinforced by the iliofemoral ligament in front, the pubofemoral anteroinferiorly and the ischiofemoral behind. Their fibres wind around the femoral neck. Extending the hip tightens this spiral arrangement and limits further extension.

That passive restraint helps keep the trunk balanced over the femoral heads while standing. Flex the hip and the spiral unwinds, making the capsule relatively lax and allowing more movement. A ligament can therefore be essential to stability without remaining equally taut in every joint position.

check.q: Why is the hip capsule tighter in standing extension than in flexion?
check.a: Extension winds up its spiral ligament fibres; flexion unwinds them.

steps.pitfall: The ligament of the femoral head is not the main restraint against hyperextension; the capsular ligaments provide that restraint.

steps.title: A small lean changes the muscle load
steps.text:
During single-leg stance, body weight acts medial to the supporting hip and tends to drop the opposite side of the pelvis. The abductors of the standing leg pull in the opposite direction to keep the pelvis level.

Leaning the trunk towards the supporting hip brings the centre of mass closer to that joint and shortens the body-weight lever arm. Less abductor force is then needed. This explains the compensatory lean in a painful or weak abductor mechanism: the posture changes the mechanical demand as well as the appearance of the gait.

check.q: Why does leaning towards a weak supporting hip reduce the work its abductors must do?
check.a: It brings body weight closer to the hip centre, shortening the lever arm that the abductors must oppose.

objectives: Describe the bony and ligamentous stability of the hip
Trace the blood supply of the femoral head
Explain why an intracapsular fracture threatens the head
Relate the spiral hip capsule to standing stability and flexion mobility
takeaways: A deep socket, a strong capsule and three named ligaments make dislocation rare.
The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest in the body and limits extension.
Retinacular vessels along the neck supply the head; an intracapsular fracture tears them.
The iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments tighten in extension and become relatively lax in flexion.

title: The ankle and the arches of the foot
summary: A mortise that is stable dorsiflexed, and three arches that carry you.

steps.title: The mortise
steps.text: Tibia and fibula grip the talus like a carpenter's mortise, held by the tibiofibular syndesmosis. The talus is wider in front, so in dorsiflexion it is wedged tight and the joint is stable; in plantar flexion it is loose – which is why you sprain your ankle going down stairs or off a kerb.

check.q: Why is the ankle most stable in dorsiflexion?
check.a: The talus is wider anteriorly, so it wedges into the mortise.

steps.title: Sprains and fractures
steps.text: Inversion injuries tear the lateral ligament, the anterior talofibular part first – the commonest ligament injury in the body. The medial (deltoid) ligament is far stronger, so an eversion force tends to avulse the medial malleolus instead of tearing the ligament.

check.q: Which ligament is torn first in an inversion injury?
check.a: The anterior talofibular ligament.

steps.title: The arches
steps.text:
A medial longitudinal arch (calcaneus – talus – navicular – cuneiforms – medial three metatarsals), a lower lateral one, and a transverse arch. They are held by bone shape, by the plantar aponeurosis and spring ligament, and by tibialis posterior and the intrinsic muscles.

The windlass mechanism tightens the aponeurosis as the toes extend at toe-off, turning a flexible foot into a rigid lever.

check.q: Which ligament is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
check.a: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament.

steps.title: The ankle is not the whole hindfoot
steps.text:
The talocrural joint is the hinge between the tibiofibular mortise and the talus. Its main movements are dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Tilting the sole inwards or outwards requires movement chiefly at the joints below and in front of the talus, especially the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

Those joint axes are oblique, so real foot movement combines rotation in several planes. The hindfoot can adapt to a sloping surface while the leg remains relatively upright. When describing an ankle injury, keep the mortise, the tibiofibular syndesmosis and the joints of the hindfoot as distinct structures.

check.q: Does inversion mainly occur at the talocrural hinge?
check.a: No. It chiefly involves the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

steps.title: A sprain above the joint line
steps.text:
The distal tibia and fibula are tied together by the syndesmosis, a fibrous connection rather than a ball-and-socket or hinge joint. It permits small adjustments while keeping the mortise appropriately fitted around the talus.

An external rotation force on the foot can injure this connection. This is the anatomical basis of a high ankle sprain: the damaged structures lie between the tibia and fibula, proximal to the talocrural joint line. It differs from the common inversion sprain involving the lateral ankle ligaments.

check.q: What distinguishes a high ankle sprain anatomically from a usual lateral inversion sprain?
check.a: A high sprain involves the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis; a lateral inversion sprain involves ligaments connecting the fibula to the talus and calcaneus.

objectives: Describe the ankle mortise and what makes it stable
Name the collateral ligaments and which is injured in an inversion sprain
Explain how the arches are supported
Separate movement at the ankle mortise from inversion and eversion below it
takeaways: The talus is wider in front, so dorsiflexion is the close-packed, stable position.
The anterior talofibular ligament is the first to tear in an inversion injury.
The deltoid ligament is so strong it avulses bone rather than tearing.
The talocrural joint mainly dorsiflexes and plantarflexes; inversion and eversion chiefly involve the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

title: The cranial nerves
summary: Twelve nerves, the holes they leave by, and a quick way to test them.

steps.title: All twelve
steps.text:
I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal.

Sensory, motor or both: Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most.

check.q: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres?
check.a: III, VII, IX and X.

steps.title: Where they leave the skull
steps.text:
Cribriform plate (I) · optic canal (II) · superior orbital fissure (III, IV, V1, VI) · foramen rotundum (V2) · foramen ovale (V3) · internal acoustic meatus (VII, VIII) · jugular foramen (IX, X, XI) · hypoglossal canal (XII).

A jugular foramen lesion therefore gives a triad: loss of gag, hoarseness and a weak shrug.

check.q: Which nerves leave through the jugular foramen?
check.a: IX, X and XI.

steps.title: The trigeminal nerve
steps.text:
Sensation to the whole face in three territories, plus the muscles of mastication through V3. Its motor fibres travel only with the mandibular division, so a V3 lesion deviates the open jaw towards the weak side.

Trigeminal neuralgia is lancinating pain in one division, typically V2 or V3, often from a vascular loop on the root.

check.q: What are the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve and which is motor?
check.a: Ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular; only the mandibular division carries motor fibres.

steps.title: The hypoglossal nerve
steps.text: Motor to all the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles. Genioglossus protrudes the tongue, so a lower motor neurone lesion makes the tongue deviate towards the weak side on protrusion – with wasting and fasciculation. An upper motor neurone lesion pushes it away from the lesion, without wasting.

check.q: The tongue deviates to the left on protrusion. Which nerve is damaged?
check.a: The left hypoglossal nerve.

steps.title: One reflex can test two nerves
steps.text:
A reflex has an afferent limb bringing information in and an efferent limb carrying a response out. In the corneal reflex, sensation travels through the nasociliary branch of V1; the response closes the eyelids through VII and orbicularis oculi on both sides.

The pupillary light reflex uses a different pair. Light information enters through II, and parasympathetic fibres travelling with III reach the ciliary ganglion and sphincter pupillae. Central connections normally make both pupils constrict when one eye is illuminated. Name the incoming and outgoing nerves separately rather than assigning an entire reflex to one nerve.

check.q: Which cranial nerves are the incoming and outgoing limbs of the corneal reflex?
check.a: V1 carries corneal sensation in; VII activates orbicularis oculi to close the eyelids.

steps.pitfall: This is a pathway exercise; do not practise touching the cornea to test it.

steps.title: Sensory, motor, or both?
steps.text:
Group the nerves by what they carry. I, II and VIII carry special sensory information. III, IV, VI, XI and XII are chiefly motor, although III also carries parasympathetic fibres. V, VII, IX and X are mixed nerves with sensory and motor components.

The mixed group explains why one lesion can combine a movement problem with a sensory deficit. A proximal vagal lesion, for example, can affect palatal movement, laryngeal movement and visceral functions. The number alone is a label; fibre types tell you the kinds of functions a lesion could interrupt.

check.q: Which four cranial nerves are classically grouped as mixed sensory and motor nerves?
check.a: V, VII, IX and X.

objectives: Name the twelve cranial nerves in order and their functional class
Give the foramen each uses
Describe a bedside test for each
Trace the sensory and motor limbs of the corneal and pupillary light reflexes
takeaways: Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More — sensory, motor or both.
III, VII, IX and X carry parasympathetic fibres.
Only the trochlear nerve leaves from the back of the brainstem.
Corneal reflex: V1 in, VII out. Pupillary light reflex: II in, parasympathetic III out.

title: The larynx
summary: Cartilages, the two nerves that matter, and what hoarseness means.

steps.title: The cartilages
steps.text: Thyroid cartilage shields the front, cricoid is the only complete ring in the whole airway – which is why cricoid pressure works and why a cricothyroidotomy is done through the membrane just above it. The paired arytenoids sit on the cricoid lamina and swivel to open and close the vocal folds.

check.q: Which is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway?
check.a: The cricoid cartilage.

steps.title: Two nerves, one muscle that matters
steps.text:
All the intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and tenses the cord.

Sensation above the cords is the internal laryngeal nerve, below the cords the recurrent – so an inhaled foreign body below the cords provokes a violent cough.

check.q: Which intrinsic muscle abducts the vocal folds?
check.a: Posterior cricoarytenoid — the only abductor.

steps.title: Why the left is at risk
steps.text:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta; the right hooks under the subclavian artery. The left therefore has a long thoracic course, and is the one paralysed by a left hilar tumour, an aortic aneurysm, a dilated left atrium or thoracic surgery.

Unilateral palsy gives hoarseness; bilateral palsy threatens the airway.

check.q: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve more often affected than the right?
check.a: It loops under the aortic arch and has a long intrathoracic course.

steps.title: Opening the airway is a muscle action
steps.text:
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds. It rotates the arytenoid cartilages so their vocal processes move apart, widening the rima glottidis for inspiration. Most other intrinsic muscles help bring the folds together or adjust their shape.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies this opener as well as most of the closers. Bilateral nerve injury can therefore compromise the airway, with the final fold position depending on the injury. The key point is mechanical: quiet breathing requires the folds to separate, while phonation requires controlled approximation and vibration.

check.q: Which intrinsic muscle is the only abductor of the vocal folds?
check.a: Posterior cricoarytenoid, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

steps.title: Pitch is not simply how wide the gap is
steps.text:
The cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage relative to the cricoid, lengthening and increasing tension in the vocal folds. This helps produce higher pitches. Thyroarytenoid and its vocalis portion make finer adjustments to length, stiffness and the vibrating edge.

Opening the folds, closing them and changing their tension are therefore different jobs. An isolated external superior laryngeal nerve injury weakens cricothyroid and can reduce pitch control even when the folds still abduct. A person may retain a conversational voice but struggle to reach high notes.

check.q: Why can external superior laryngeal nerve injury impair high notes without paralysing vocal-fold abduction?
check.a: It affects cricothyroid and fold tension; posterior cricoarytenoid, the abductor, has recurrent laryngeal supply.

objectives: Name the laryngeal cartilages and the joints between them
Explain the actions of the intrinsic muscles on the vocal folds
Give the sensory and motor supply above and below the folds
Distinguish vocal-fold abduction from tension and relate each to the responsible muscle
takeaways: All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor — the only one that opens the airway.
The cricothyroid membrane is the emergency airway.
Posterior cricoarytenoid opens the vocal folds; cricothyroid lengthens and tenses them. Recurrent laryngeal injury can affect opening as well as voice.

title: The ear
summary: Three compartments, one chain of bones, and where hearing fails.

steps.title: Outer and middle
steps.text:
The external canal ends at the tympanic membrane. Beyond it the middle ear contains the ossicular chain – malleus, incus, stapes – which turns large low-pressure air movements into small high-pressure fluid movements, a gain of about 20 times.

The Eustachian tube ventilates it; in children it is shorter and more horizontal, which is why they get otitis media.

check.q: What do the three ossicles achieve?
check.a: Impedance matching — amplifying vibration about twentyfold so it can move fluid in the cochlea.

steps.title: The inner ear
steps.text: The cochlea for hearing and the vestibule and semicircular canals for balance, all filled with perilymph and endolymph. The cochlea is tonotopic: high frequencies at the stiff, narrow base, low frequencies at the floppy apex – so noise damage and presbyacusis hit high tones first.

check.q: Which part of the inner ear detects rotation, and which detects linear acceleration?
check.a: The semicircular canals detect rotation; the utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration.

steps.title: Conductive versus sensorineural
steps.text:
Rinne: normally air conduction beats bone conduction. If bone beats air, the fault is conductive.
Weber: a tuning fork on the vertex localises to a conductive loss and away from a sensorineural one.

Conductive causes sit in the canal or middle ear – wax, effusion, otosclerosis. Sensorineural causes sit in the cochlea or VIII – noise, age, an acoustic neuroma.

check.q: Weber's test lateralises to the right and Rinne is negative on the right. What kind of deafness?
check.a: Right conductive deafness.

steps.title: One window pushes, the other gives
steps.text:
The stapes footplate moves at the oval window, transmitting vibration into the fluid of the inner ear. Fluid is nearly incompressible, so another boundary must yield. The round window membrane supplies that flexibility, allowing pressure changes to displace the cochlear fluids.

A travelling wave moves the basilar membrane and bends the sensory hair bundles through relative motion within the organ of Corti. The hair cells convert mechanical movement into an electrical signal carried onward by the cochlear division of VIII. A vibrating eardrum is only the beginning of this chain.

check.q: What would be lost if the cochlea had a rigid wall where the round window should be?
check.a: The compliant outlet needed for effective fluid displacement when the stapes moves at the oval window.

steps.title: Turning and tilting are different signals
steps.text:
The semicircular ducts signal angular acceleration: changes in head rotation. Their three roughly perpendicular planes let them detect turns in different directions. Movement of endolymph deflects the cupula and the hair bundles in each ampulla.

The utricle and saccule instead use otolith organs to signal linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity. Their weighted membranes shift relative to the hair cells. Turning the head and leaning it sideways can feel like one movement, but the vestibular apparatus analyses different components with different sensors.

check.q: Which receptors distinguish a car accelerating straight ahead from the head beginning to turn?
check.a: The otolith organs signal linear acceleration; the semicircular ducts signal angular acceleration.

objectives: Divide the ear into its three parts and name the contents of each
Trace sound from the auricle to the cochlear nerve
Distinguish conductive from sensorineural deafness
Explain why the cochlea needs both an oval window and a round window
takeaways: Malleus, incus, stapes amplify about twentyfold to overcome the impedance of fluid.
The middle ear is an air space connected to the nasopharynx by the pharyngotympanic tube.
Rinne and Weber separate conductive from sensorineural loss at the bedside.
Stapes drives the oval window; the round window permits fluid displacement, allowing a travelling wave to move the cochlear partition.

title: The pelvic floor
summary: The muscular hammock, and what happens when it gives way.

steps.title: Levator ani
steps.text:
The pelvic diaphragm is mostly levator ani – puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus – slung from the pubis to the coccyx and to the tendinous arch on obturator internus. It supports the pelvic viscera and maintains continence.

Puborectalis forms a sling behind the anorectal junction; its tone creates the anorectal angle, and relaxing it straightens the angle for defaecation.

check.q: Which part of levator ani maintains the anorectal angle?
check.a: Puborectalis, slinging round the anorectal junction.

steps.title: Nerve supply and childbirth
steps.text:
Levator ani is supplied from the sacral plexus (S3–S4) and by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) – S2, 3, 4 keep the guts off the floor.

Stretch or tearing during childbirth, or a pudendal neuropathy, weakens the floor and leads to prolapse and stress incontinence. A pudendal nerve block is placed at the ischial spine, reached through the vagina.

check.q: Which nerve roots supply levator ani?
check.a: S3–S4 directly, with a contribution from the pudendal nerve (S2–S4).

steps.title: The perineum
steps.text:
A diamond split by a line between the ischial tuberosities into a urogenital triangle in front – with the deep perineal pouch and the external urethral sphincter – and an anal triangle behind, containing the ischio-anal fossae.

Those fossae are fat-filled potential spaces that communicate behind the anal canal, which is why an abscess in one can spread to the other in a horseshoe.

check.q: Which nerve supplies the perineum, and where can it be blocked?
check.a: The pudendal nerve, blocked at the ischial spine.

steps.title: Support has to leave room for openings
steps.text:
A pelvic floor cannot be an unbroken sheet: the urethra and anal canal must pass through it, with the vagina also passing through the anterior opening in female anatomy. The medial fibres of levator ani support the margins of these openings while allowing them to change shape.

The perineal body is a fibromuscular meeting point between the urogenital and anal regions. Several perineal muscles and fibres related to the anal sphincter and levator ani attach here. Its integrity helps keep the floor and perineum connected, so an injury can impair support even without interrupting every muscle.

check.q: Why can damage to a small perineal body have effects beyond that one point?
check.a: It is a shared attachment where several muscular and fascial supports meet.

steps.title: The sling and the two sphincters
steps.text:
Puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction forwards and maintains its angle. The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle providing involuntary tone; the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under somatic control. These are related mechanisms, not three names for one structure.

During defaecation, relaxation of the sling reduces the angle while coordinated sphincter relaxation opens the outlet. When continence is required, the angle and sphincter pressures work together. The pelvic floor also responds to rises in abdominal pressure, such as coughing, to support the pelvic viscera.

check.q: Which component creates the anorectal angle, and which anal sphincter is skeletal muscle?
check.a: Puborectalis creates the angle; the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle.

objectives: Name the muscles of the pelvic diaphragm and their attachments
Explain how the floor maintains continence
Describe what happens when it fails
Explain how levator ani, the perineal body and sphincters contribute different parts of continence
takeaways: Levator ani is the floor: puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus.
Puborectalis slings round the anorectal junction and holds the anorectal angle.
Nerve supply is S3–S4 directly and the pudendal nerve.
Pelvic support, the puborectalis sling and the urethral and anal sphincters cooperate; continence does not depend on one muscle alone.
